children: China's foreign exchange reserves rose slightly in October, against the backdrop of a strong Chinese currency that recently climbed to a multiyear high against the dollar thanks to strong exports.

The country's hoard of foreign exchange rose by $4.9 billion to $3.405 trillion at the end of October, the People's Bank of China said Saturday. Economists surveyed by The Wall Street Journal expected end-October foreign exchange reserves of $3.41 trillion.

Largely unfazed by weak domestic economic data, the yuan climbed to a four-year high against the greenback in recent weeks. To tame the rally, the People's Bank of China tweaked forex reserve rules on Tuesday, requiring Chinese financial institutions to lock up more foreign-currency deposits with the central bank.

By tightening onshore dollar liquidity, the measure should moderate rather than reverse the yuan's appreciation, given strong export demand, according to Moody's Ratings. "The effect on exports will be small but positive, mainly by easing margin pressure on lower-end exporters," the agency's analysts said in a note this week.

ING economist Lynn Song suggests that raising the forex reserve requirement ratio for financial institutions signals the PBOC is pushing back against the speed of the yuan's appreciation. He also notes the action is largely symbolic, stopping short of a sharp intervention like aggressively adjusting the currency's daily reference rate.

While Beijing has been greenlighting yuan's gradual rise, analysts say the PBOC's move this week is a clear sign that policymakers have no appetite for a fast currency appreciation that would dent Chinese exporters' global competitiveness.

Extending its buying streak to two full years, China's central bank boosted its gold holdings in October to 78.3 million troy ounces, up from 77.47 million the previous month, data released Saturday showed.
